newsitem.title: FRANCE: Monaco's Rainier rules out abrupt abdication.
newsitem.headline: Monaco's Rainier rules out abrupt abdication.

text.p: Prince Rainier of Monaco has ruled out abdicating after 47 years in power, saying he is grooming his son Prince Albert to take over gradually in the miniature Riviera principality.

"I've made a deal with Albert. I'm waiting for my son to feel ready to take over," Rainier told the weekly Le Figaro Magazine in an interview to appear on Saturday. "I don't want a brutal abdication. It must be done smoothly."
Prince Albert, who is 38, "should increasingly step up his activities, his decisions. I would not like to live through a big abdication ceremony but rather a gradual transfer of powers," he said.

Rainier, who is 73 and underwent heart bypass surgery two years ago, has been rebuffing speculation he will abdicate ever since the death of his wife, former Hollywood actress Princess Grace, in a 1982 car crash.

"In 1997, I will myself preside over the 700th anniversary of the arrival of the Grimaldi on the rock of Monaco," he said. The prince had himself spurred speculation on his abdication by putting Albert in charge of the celebrations.
Rainier's Grimaldi dynasty has ruled Monaco, the smallest U.N. member state in size and with just 5,000 citizens, since an ancestor wrested control of a Genoese-held fortress in 1297.
Albert has said in the past he believes his initiation is complete.

Le Figaro said Rainier, jolted by scandals including the divorce this year of his daughter Stephanie after her husband was photographed in a sex romp with a Belgian stripper, may even secretly want to stay at least until his 50th anniversary in power in 1999.
Rainier, a shy but forceful ruler who transformed Monaco from a gambling paradise into a booming international business centre, also described his palace overlooking the Mediterranean.
"What I like about this palace is that it's not Buckingham," he said, referring to British Queen Elizabeth's palace in London. "It's not immense. It's a palace on a human scale."
"I want my children and grandchildren to come here often, but I know that Prince Albert is very attached to the place and likes living here," he said.

He also said that palace workers formed a sort of family. "They all want to serve the prince well. And after all, they form an aristocracy: working in the palace is a privilege, to stay there is a consecration!"
